transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-07-22
Start time: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Carlos Rivera (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (VectorStream CTO), Ben Ortiz (VectorStream ML Engineer), Samir Patel (VectorStream Infra Lead)

Summary (auto): initial latency/throughput discovery; follow-ups: benchmark run, security review, pricing/SLOs

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on this account. We also have Carlos, our SE, who'll handle the deep bench and infra questions. How's everyone doing?
[00:05] Aisha: Doing good, thanks. Quick intro — I'm Aisha, CTO at VectorStream, we build low-latency real-time assistants for logistics ops. Ben and Samir are with me.
[00:12] Ben: hey
[00:13] Samir: hi all
[00:15] Carlos: great to meet you. Can you give us the primary performance goals so we can focus the convo? p95, concurrency, streaming specifics?
[00:22] Aisha: Yeah, our target is pretty aggressive — for our streaming chat UI we want around 150-200ms p95 token latency for short responses, and end-to-end p95 under 350ms for most common prompts. Concurrently we expect bursts to 300-400 active users during peaks, sustained 80-120 during normal hours.
[00:40] Maya: that's really helpful. payload size? are responses short (20-40 tokens) or longer?
[00:46] Ben: most responses are short, 20-60 tokens, some longer analytic outputs up to 400 tokens but they're less frequent. We also do few-shot prompts occasionally.
[00:56] Carlos: ok, that maps to two different profiles — short streaming responses where per-token latency matters and longer completions that are more throughput-bound. Are you currently running any public cloud LLM infra?
[01:06] Aisha: We're using Hosted APIs today (vendor X) but cost and latency variability is a problem. We want to evaluate Dedicated or Private for predictable performance. Also need SOC2 and audit logs for enterprise customers.
[01:18] Samir: also network egress and data residency are concerns for some clients.
[01:22] Maya: understood. On the performance side, a few considerations: streaming p95 depends on model size, quantization, serving backend, and batching. We often achieve 100-200ms per-token p95 on smaller quantized models on Dedicated hardware with streaming optimizations, but bigger models will be higher. Also, continuous batching helps throughput but can add latency depending on your SLOs.
[01:38] Ben: can you explain the tradeoff? if we need 200ms p95, does batching kill us?
[01:44] Carlos: good question. Batching increases tokens/sec and reduces cost but introduces a batch-wait window. Redwood's runtime uses adaptive batching and latency-aware routing — we can set max batch wait times or prioritize low-latency requests into smaller batches or single-request execution. For Dedicated you can reserve capacity and tune batch sizes to hit your p95. We also do KV/prefix caching which reduces compute for repeated prompts and long contexts.
[02:08] Aisha: KV cache — does that mean long conversations are faster after warm-up?
[02:12] Carlos: Exactly — prefix KV cache keeps past key/value states so subsequent tokens don't need to recompute earlier attention, which reduces per-token latency for continuing conversations. Cold-starts still pay the initial cost.
[02:22] Samir: what's the cold-start hit typically? hundreds ms? seconds?
[02:25] Carlos: depends on model size and quantization. For a 7B quantized model, cold-start for the first token can be 300-700ms on some hardware; for 13B it's higher. But with warm KV and right routing, steady-state per-token can be under 150ms for smaller models. We'll provide concrete numbers in the benchmark.
[02:41] Ben: tokens/sec — what's realistic for Dedicated vs Hosted?
[02:44] Maya: Hosted varies because multi-tenant load and routing, our published profiles give ranges. Dedicated gives you predictable tokens/sec per GPU pool. For example, on a 8-GPU Dedicated pool with a 7B quantized model we typically see Xk tokens/sec at saturation — we'll run your workload to measure.
[03:00] Aisha: ok, we need numbers — p95 at our target concurrency 300-400. Is that feasible?
[03:05] Carlos: feasibility depends on concurrency vs think-time. If users stream slowly with think-time between requests, the effective concurrency on the model may be lower. But if they're all actively streaming, you'll need capacity planning: reserve N GPUs to handle peak rps. We usually simulate with your prompt mix to estimate GPUs needed for p95 targets. That's what the benchmark run will do.
[03:25] Samir: networking — will we see variability from VPC peering and customer network?
[03:29] Maya: network adds variability. For Private (VPC/on-prem) you get control over VPC placement and can avoid public internet hops; Dedicated reduces multi-tenant interference and we can co-locate in your chosen region. We'll include network RTT in the benchmark.
[03:43] Ben: are there any built-in tools to measure p95 and token cost in Redwood Console?
[03:47] Maya: Yes, Console provides per-route P50/P95/P99 latency, token-level cost breakdown, and tracing hooks. We also expose per-model throughput metrics and request-level logs.
[03:57] Aisha: security — SOC2 and KMS for keys, we need audit logs and SSO.
[04:02] Maya: Redwood supports SOC2 controls, KMS integrations, audit logs, and SAML SSO. For Private deployments we can do customer-managed KMS and air-gapped options. We'll schedule a security deep-dive next week as noted.
[04:16] Carlos: for benchmarking, we'll need: your prompt corpus, tokenization notes (how you count tokens), target concurrency profile, and any cold-start vs warm conversation split. We'll run both streaming and non-streaming tests.
[04:28] Ben: I'll upload the corpus by Thursday. We have about 2,000 representative prompts and a synthetic concurrency trace.
[04:33] Maya: perfect. Our benchmark approach: 1) run small-scale token/sec test to validate model variant and quantization, 2) run sustained concurrency simulations with real prompt mixes, 3) run streaming latency measurements capturing p95 per-token and end-to-end response times, 4) provide cost estimates and GPU count recommendations.
[04:52] Aisha: Do you recommend Dedicated or Private for us? latency and enterprise controls are both important.
[04:57] Carlos: For most customers with strict p95 and enterprise controls, Dedicated is the sweet spot — you get reserved capacity, predictable performance, and we can still provide SOC2 level controls and private networking. Private (VPC/on-prem) is for customers with regulatory or ultra-sensitive data needs; it carries additional ops effort. We can present tradeoffs with numbers after the benchmark.
[05:16] Samir: any quick ballpark on cost uplift from Hosted to Dedicated?
[05:19] Maya: Dedicated is typically higher fixed cost but lower per-token variability; it often pays off if you have steady high volume. We'll include a few pricing scenarios against your workload.
[05:28] Ben: quantization — does 4-bit quantization impact latency significantly?
[05:31] Carlos: Quantization reduces memory and can improve throughput; latency effects depend on kernels. Some 4-bit paths are slightly faster per-token; others require more compute for dequant/compensation. We'll include comparisons in the run.
[05:45] Aisha: great. If we run with a smaller quantized model to hit p95, what about quality regressions?
[05:50] Maya: that's a key tradeoff. Redwood Optimize includes eval hooks so you can run quality checks on your prompt sets and detect regressions when you change model/quantization. We'll show how to tie those eval results to rollout policies.
[06:02] Ben: demo? can we see Console metrics and previous benchmarks?
[06:05] Maya: yes, we'll share a short demo recording and a sample benchmark report. Carlos will run a custom benchmark for you after we get your corpus.
[06:12] Carlos: one more note on streaming: we support chunked responses and smaller token emission sizes to keep perceived latency low; we can tune chunk sizes in the runtime.
[06:20] Samir: good to know. Any blockers we should be aware of?
[06:23] Aisha: primary blockers are security sign-off and cost approval. We'll need concrete SLOs and a cost model to present to procurement.
[06:30] Maya: understood. We'll aim to provide benchmark numbers and a few pricing scenarios so you can take that to procurement.
[06:36] Aisha: timeline — we'd like a pilot in August, ideally start with Dedicated pilot early August.
[06:41] Maya: sounds doable pending benchmark outcomes and security review. We'll try to get the benchmark results by end of the week after we get your corpus.
[06:47] Ben: I'll upload corpus and tokenization notes today/tomorrow.
[06:50] Maya: great. Recap of next steps: Redwood runs Dedicated benchmark with VectorStream prompt set; share pricing + SLOs; schedule security deep-dive; customer uploads corpus and concurrency profile.
[06:59] Aisha: thanks everyone, clear next steps.
[07:02] Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up with calendar invites and links to the shared folder.

End of call.

Notes on transcription: occasional overlaps and filler words removed for readability; some proper nouns (model names, vendor names) may be approximated in the transcript.
